walkthroughs.body_html:
Sustaining Ecosystems — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Sustaining Ecosystems brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Sustaining Ecosystems.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Why does plastic accumulate in ocean gyres?
options: The 'Great Pacific Garbage Patch' is a solid floating island of plastic you can walk on.

Gyres are large rotating ocean currents driven by wind and Coriolis effect; floating debris is carried in but the rotation traps it in the centre, where currents are weak, concentrating plastic over decades.
Plastic accumulates in gyres because the water there is denser.
Stratified sampling means picking samples from different strata of rock.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between random, stratified and systematic sampling?
options: Four-figure references are for OS maps and six-figure references are for atlases.

Random: every member has equal chance of selection. Systematic: pick every nth item. Stratified: divide the population into groups and sample proportionally from each — ensures subgroup representation.
All three sampling methods produce the same results.
Stratified sampling means picking samples from different strata of rock.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a four-figure and six-figure grid reference?
options: Four-figure references identify a 1km square (eastings then northings); six-figure references pinpoint a location within that square to 100m accuracy by adding tenths.
Four-figure references are for OS maps and six-figure references are for atlases.
Plastic accumulates in gyres because the water there is denser.
Six-figure references are just longer versions of the same thing.
